SYNTHETIC TEST DOCUMENT - FICTIONAL PATIENT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE
Gastroscopy Then Colonoscopy in One Sitting
Hensley Narrows Surgery Center (fictional)
Facility category: ambulatory surgical center, POS 24
Date performed: October 19, 2026
Person examined: Petronella Szymanski-Abara (fictional), 64-year-old woman
Gastroenterologist: Lazare Sobczak-Muir, DO (fictional)
Sedation and airway: propofol given by Wynona Tarkington-Ezeh, CRNA (fictional), of Hensley Anesthesia
Collective (fictional), which bills separately
Why Both Were Done
Six kilograms of unintended weight loss over five months, with early satiety. CT of the abdomen at Ostley Imaging
(fictional) on September 28, 2026 suggested a filling defect in the gastric antrum. She has never had a
colonoscopy. Both examinations were done to look for a cause.
Stomach and Duodenum
The gastroscope was introduced by mouth under visual guidance and steered through the stomach and pylorus
into the second part of the duodenum. Esophageal mucosa looked healthy throughout. On the greater curvature
of the antrum sat a 14 mm pedunculated polyp with a lobulated head on a short, thick stalk (Paris 0-Ip). A hot
snare was closed around the stalk 5 mm below the head; with blended current the polyp was transected at the
stalk and retrieved with a net. The stalk base was clean and dry, so no clip was needed. The rest of the stomach
and the duodenum looked normal. No other upper tract tissue was taken.
Large Bowel
Preparation was excellent, Boston score 9. The colonoscope reached the cecum, where its landmarks, the
appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve, were photographed; withdrawal lasted 12 minutes. In the rectum, 4 and 6
cm from the anal verge, there were two 3 mm pale, flat polyps with a hyperplastic surface pattern. That optical
diagnosis was made with high confidence, so both were left in place: no polypectomy was performed in the colon
and no colonic biopsy was taken. Scattered sigmoid diverticula. The retroflexed rectal view was otherwise normal.
At a Glance
1. 14 mm pedunculated antral polyp, removed with a hot snare and sent for histology.
2. Two diminutive hyperplastic-appearing rectal polyps, deliberately not removed.
3. Sigmoid diverticulosis; no colonic cause for the weight loss.
Next Steps
The antral polyp goes to Corbridge Pathology Group (fictional), which reports it separately. Office review of the
histology in about two weeks. If the weight loss continues despite benign results, CT of the chest will be
considered. Next colonoscopy in ten years if nothing changes.
Report authenticated: Lazare Sobczak-Muir, DO (fictional), October 19, 2026 11:52
